name: Taiyuan Wusu International Airport
before:
Shanxi's main airport and the largest in the province, about 15 km south east of downtown Taiyuan. For anything in this part of northern China it is the practical arrival point rather than routing through Beijing and driving.

The field is older than most Chinese airports still in use. It was surveyed in 1939 and built the same year on ground near Wusu village, which gave the airport its name, and opened that November as a joint military and civilian airfield. It has been rebuilt and extended repeatedly since.

It remains a joint use airport, so parts of the site are not public and photography restrictions apply in a way they would not at a purely commercial terminal.
after:
Shanxi's main airport and the largest in the province, about 15 km south east of downtown Taiyuan. It handled about 14.6 million passengers in 2025.

An expansion has added a second runway, and a new terminal is being built.

claims.note: Replaces "rebuilt and extended repeatedly since". The Phase III expansion (under way since the end of 2021) includes a second 3,600 m runway, which Wikipedia says came into use on 25 December 2025, when the first was closed for renovation. The date and the closure are not in the text: Wikipedia's source for them, the Shanxi provincial government's page, answered 503 and then 502 through the browser, and the one other source (a Tencent News aviation columnist, 2 May 2026) says the second runway is built and in use but gives no date. OurAirports' runway table lists both runways.

claims.claim: surveyed and built in 1939 near Wusu village, which gave it its name; opened November 1939 as a joint military and civilian airfield
claims.wasBefore: It was surveyed in 1939 and built the same year on ground near Wusu village, which gave the airport its name, and opened that November as a joint military and civilian airfield.
claims.why: Only Wikipedia. Its own history also says the field went to military use in 1948 and reopened as a civil airport on 1 July 1971, the opening date in its infobox, so the 1939 story needs a second source before it is told. None reachable: the airport group's old site (sxairport.org.cn) answers 503, Chinese government pages 502, and the WeChat posts Wikipedia cites sit behind a verification wall.

claims.wasBefore: It has been rebuilt and extended repeatedly since.
claims.why: Goes with the history above; replaced by the current expansion, which two sources support.

claims.claim: remains a joint use airport; parts not public; photography restrictions
claims.wasBefore: It remains a joint use airport, so parts of the site are not public and photography restrictions apply in a way they would not at a purely commercial terminal.
claims.why: Not supported. Wikipedia now says the 1939 field was joint military and civilian, went to military use in 1948 and was handed to the civil aviation administration in 1969; nothing says it is joint use today, and no source mentions photography rules.
